title: Interactive Examples
text: This gallery presents selected interactive and animated examples from my work in statistical methodology, biomedical visualization and teaching. Each example is designed to make a complex quantitative idea directly explorable.

title: Interactive Examples
text:
Interactive clinical reporting table


 Synthetic baseline-characteristics table
This example demonstrates a user-facing clinical reporting table designed for efficient review. Search, display density and light/dark presentation can be changed directly in the table.
The example was rebuilt specifically for this public portfolio. Every label, group size and numerical value is simulated; it contains no study name, treatment identity, sponsor, therapeutic indication or patient data.

title: Interactive Examples
text:
Interactive adverse-event summary


 Synthetic safety-review table
This example demonstrates a compact user-facing overview of adverse events, organized into occurrence, severity, serious outcomes and focused-review categories. Search, display density and light/dark presentation can be changed directly in the table.
The table was rebuilt specifically for this public portfolio. Every event definition, group size and numerical value is simulated; it contains no study name, treatment identity, sponsor, therapeutic indication, coding version or patient data.

title: Interactive Examples
text:
Longitudinal analysis with statistical signals


 Synthetic visit-by-visit model table
This example combines observed values, change from baseline and repeated-measures model results across visits. The primary estimate in each descriptive cell is emphasized, while SD remains visually secondary.
Inferential signals are coordinated across the result: green identifies p-values below 0.05 and their corresponding confidence intervals; orange identifies p-values from 0.05 to below 0.10 and the related intervals. All outcomes, visits, group sizes and estimates are simulated.

title: Interactive Examples
text:
Acceptance checks and issue traceability


 Synthetic acceptance-review matrix
This example shows how acceptance checks can connect each finding to its output, issue category, evidence, decision and required action. It brings numerical validation together with checks of populations, denominators, derivations, statistical presentation, specifications and reproducibility.
The issue patterns reflect realistic findings encountered during independent table and listing validation, but the output names, counts, values and wording have been rebuilt for this public portfolio. All content is synthetic and study-neutral; it contains no study, sponsor, treatment, indication or participant information.

title: Interactive Examples
text:
Interactive change-from-baseline distributions


 Synthetic patient-level violin plots
This example presents patient-level change from baseline by visit and group. The violin shapes show the full distributions, with medians and interquartile ranges retained as precise visual anchors.
Explore individual values: hover over a point to inspect its synthetic subject identifier, group, visit and change from baseline. The yellow diamond marks a synthetic review value, while the dashed lines provide illustrative review limits. Every visit, identifier and value is simulated.

title: Interactive Examples
text:
Mean profile with 95% confidence intervals


 Coordinated summary of the same synthetic data
The group-specific mean profiles and 95% confidence intervals below summarize exactly the same simulated patient-level values as the violin plots.
Explore the estimates: hover over a marker to see the mean, 95% confidence interval and number of simulated observations at that visit.

title: Interactive Examples
text:
Interactive survival curves


 Synthetic time-to-event analysis
This example presents two Kaplan–Meier-style survival curves as separated step functions with stepwise 95% confidence bands and a corresponding numbers-at-risk table below.
Explore across time: move over the plot to inspect the nearest failure or censoring time. Failures use the stronger Group A or Group B tone; censoring marks use the related lighter tone. Controls can hide the confidence bands or either marker type, and the figure follows the website’s light/dark theme.
All event times, censoring times, survival estimates, confidence intervals and risk counts are simulated.

title: Interactive Examples
text:
Coloured 3D nose: local surface shape


An interactive example from my face3d R package
This example uses the packaged, de-identified facial template from face3d, an R package for three-dimensional facial morphometrics and statistical shape analysis. The nasal surface is coloured by shape index, which summarizes local surface form from concave through saddle-shaped to convex regions.
The mesh contains 1,317 unique surface points connected into 2,498 triangles, revealing the local surface structure in detail. Dark red lines show stored anatomical nasal curves, while teal points identify anatomical landmarks.
Explore the model: drag to rotate, scroll or pinch to zoom, and use two fingers or the secondary mouse button to move the surface.
View the public face3d repository →

The example illustrates how statistical computation, anatomical annotation and interactive graphics can be combined in a reproducible analytical workflow. Additional examples will be added selectively from my work in statistical inference, linear models, multivariate analysis and clinical visualization.

title: Interactive Examples
text:
Triangulated 3D signal surface


 An interactive example from my diegr R package
This example uses the de-identified high-density EEG example data included with diegr. The package constructs the complete triangulated HCGSN256 three-dimensional head mesh and interpolates the sensor-level signal directly across the curved scalp surface.
The head geometry preserves the three-dimensional sensor template using 2,602 mesh points connected into 5,009 triangles, while surface colour encodes the interpolated signal. The symmetric blue–white–red scale is generated by diegr::create_scale(): blue represents negative signal, white is centred at zero and red represents positive signal. The exterior is intentionally shown as a clean coloured surface; the triangulated grid is recessed just inside the scalp and becomes visible from the internal view.
Explore the surface: drag to rotate, scroll or pinch to zoom, and use two fingers or the secondary mouse button to move it. Rotate beneath the open lower boundary to inspect the internal triangulation.
View the public diegr repository →

title: Interactive Examples
text:
Power function and changing density


 Original animation from my Statistical Inference book
These two continuously coordinated panels illustrate the exact power of a two-sided test for a normal mean with known variance.

Power function: the red point moves continuously along the exact two-sided power curve as the true effect \(\mu-\mu_0\) changes.
Changing density: the alternative normal density moves continuously relative to the fixed null distribution and critical boundaries. Its shaded volume in the rejection region changes simultaneously and is exactly the power shown on the left.

The animation connects two views of the same quantity: power as a function of the true effect and power as the probability of rejection under the corresponding alternative distribution.


 


How to read the animation: follow the red point on the power curve. At every position, the alternative density on the right changes continuously, and its shaded volume beyond the two orange critical values equals the power indicated by the point.

title: Interactive Examples
text:
Detection limits and mechanical substitution


 An animated example based on my Statistical Inference book
This animation develops Example 7.38: Bias caused by mechanical handling of nondetects. Laboratory concentrations follow a lognormal distribution, and the detection limit moves continuously across the latent population.

Latent concentration: the orange line is the current limit of detection (LoD). The red area contains values that would be reported only as nondetects; its probability grows as the LoD increases.
Mean estimation: the right panel follows the repeated-sampling distributions of the complete-data benchmark, detected values only, replacement of nondetects by zero, and replacement by LoD/2. The vertical reference line is the true population mean.

The animation makes the resulting bias visible. Detected values only systematically overestimate the mean, while substitution by zero or LoD/2 imposes artificial values and produces method-dependent distortion.


 


Key message: a nondetect is censored information—not a measured zero and not an ordinary missing value. A defensible analysis should represent the observation mechanism rather than silently manufacture measurements.

title: Interactive Examples
text:
Sequential design: triangular test


 A patient-by-patient animation from my Statistical Inference book
This animation develops Example 25.4: Triangular test for a normal mean. Ten successive patient heights are monitored for \(H_0:\mu=180\) against the one-sided alternative \(H_1:\mu\geq185\), using \(\alpha=0.01\), \(\beta=0.10\) and known variance \(\sigma^2=16\).

Triangular continuation region: the unequal stopping boundaries converge at a finite maximum information value. The accumulating path is shown in the information and score coordinates \((v_n,z_n)\).
Patient-by-patient monitoring: each frame adds one patient, updates the cumulative mean and extends the evidence path. The highlighted point is the current analysis.
Stopping decision: the path remains inside the continuation region through patient 9 and crosses the upper boundary after patient 10, terminating the study in favour of the specified one-sided alternative.

The example makes the stopping rule part of the design: the decision depends on the complete monitored path and its prespecified boundaries, not on repeatedly applying an ordinary fixed-sample test.


 


Design result: continue after each of the first nine patients; stop after patient 10 when the score path crosses the upper boundary. If no earlier crossing occurred, the converging triangular boundaries would still guarantee termination at the maximum information value.

title: Research & Publications
text:
My research connects statistical methodology with biomedical questions across clinical trials, neuroimmunology, neurodegeneration, biomarkers, omics, medical imaging and statistical shape analysis. I have contributed to more than 130 peer-reviewed publications. As of 4 October 2026, Scopus records 79 documents, 2,044 citations and an h-index of 23; the Web of Science Core Collection records 91 documents, 1,637 citations and an h-index of 21.
Explore the thematic publication record → View my Scopus profile →
The unifying principle across this work is the disciplined construction of evidence. Scientific design, measurement, data validation, modelling, computation, software, visualization and interpretation are strongest when they form one coherent system. This perspective connects my methodological research with clinical and biological applications rather than treating them as separate tracks.

title: Clinical Development
text:
Experience by development phase

Preclinical and translational research
I have long-standing experience designing and analysing controlled animal experiments and translational biomarker studies in neuroimmunology, neurodegeneration and tau pathology. This includes longitudinal designs, biomarkers, proteomics, microRNA and other high-dimensional data. I also developed end-to-end reproducible workflows for a pharmaceutical preclinical animal study, from raw-data validation through analysis, visualization and reporting.


Phase I and Ib
My early-phase work includes first-in-human studies, single-ascending-dose clinical-pharmacology studies, dose escalation, active dose comparisons and longer-term follow-up. Therapeutic areas include oncology, neuroimmunology, metabolic disease, endocrinology and immunology. Treatment modalities have included cellular and cytokine-based immunotherapy and tau immunotherapy. Responsibilities have included design strategy, simulations, protocol and SAP input and review, safety, PK/PD, immunogenicity, biomarker analysis and senior statistical review.


Phase I/II
I have supported combined dose-escalation and expansion studies in oncology using CAR-T-cell therapy, antibody-drug conjugates and dendritic-cell immunotherapy. The cancer indications included hepatocellular, lung, gastric, gastroesophageal-junction, pancreatic and prostate cancers, together with liposarcoma, Merkel-cell carcinoma and other biomarker-defined advanced solid tumors. The work has covered Bayesian and conventional design simulations, cohort and dose-escalation strategy, dose-escalation charters and meeting presentations, safety, efficacy, PK/PD, biomarkers and integrated decision support.


Phase II
My Phase II experience includes proof-of-concept and efficacy studies in oncology and neuroimmunology. I contributed to single-arm and controlled designs, biomarker-defined cohorts, longitudinal cognitive outcomes and a Bayesian adaptive proof-of-concept study in Guillain–Barré syndrome, an acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy. Work has included protocol and SAP development, estimands, missing-data simulations, TLFs, analysis, interpretation and publication.


Phase II/III
I contributed statistical sections for synopses and protocols and performed statistical analyses for randomized active-controlled oncology studies across localized, non-metastatic and metastatic disease settings. The principal outcomes included progression, survival and safety.


Phase III
My Phase III portfolio includes global randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies in autoimmune and inflammatory disease, nephrology and dermatology; a placebo-controlled Phase III oncology study; an acute-pain study; and an active-controlled pediatric vaccine program. My work includes statistical programming and review, SDTM and ADaM review, TLFs, pooled analyses, subgroup and longitudinal modelling, predictive modelling, senior statistical review and reproducible reporting.


Phase IV
As Lead Statistician for a cardiovascular Phase IV study at Charles University, I developed an end-to-end reproducible workflow covering data processing, validation, statistical analysis, visualization and publication-ready outputs. I performed and interpreted the analyses and contributed extensively to the scientific manuscript.


Real-world evidence and registries
My RWE experience includes two prospective non-interventional studies: one spanning dermatology and rheumatology, and a multicountry study in immunology, dermatology and allergology, together with long-term work on a national orthopedic arthroplasty registry. Responsibilities include effectiveness and safety analyses, treatment patterns, quality of life, healthcare-resource use, longitudinal follow-up, data quality, implant usage and survival, annual reporting and interactive applications.

title: Clinical Development
section: Responsibilities grouped by type of engagement
text:
Responsibilities grouped by type of engagement

Statistical leadership in early-phase oncology
As Lead Statistician, I provided statistical leadership across study design, conduct, analysis and reporting. Responsibilities included protocol development and review, Bayesian and conventional design simulations, dose-escalation strategy, dose-escalation charters and meeting presentations, SAPs and TLF shells, review of data-management documentation, and development and review of SDTM and ADaM specifications. I reviewed and validated SAS programs and supported efficacy, safety, PK/PD, biomarker and exploratory analyses, DSURs/ASRs, CSRs, public trial-registration submissions and scientific publications.


Statistical programming and data science in global programs
I provide statistical-programming and data-science support across global Phase III and RWE programs. My work includes programming and review of efficacy and safety analyses, pooled and subgroup analyses, longitudinal modelling, and exploratory and predictive modelling. I extensively review SDTM and ADaM datasets and specifications, review define.xml, and program or review TLFs. I also review and validate SAS programs, reproduce selected analyses in R, and develop reproducible and interactive reporting solutions.


Lead programming for a prospective RWE study
As Lead Statistical Programmer, I am responsible for validation and independent double programming of TLFs and senior review of data-management and statistical documentation. I review SDTM and ADaM datasets, specifications and related study data, help ensure consistency across protocol, analysis requirements, data structures and outputs, and design and program an R Shiny application supporting interactive study review.


Lead statistical review within a CRO
As Lead Statistician within a CRO, I provided statistical leadership and review across Phase I and Phase III studies. This included review of protocols, SAPs, TLF shells, statistical methods, programs and outputs, together with review of safety, efficacy, PK/PD, corrected-QT or immunogenicity results, as applicable.


Neurodegeneration and integrated biomarkers
I provided senior statistical and bioinformatics leadership across Phase I and II clinical, cognitive, language, functional, safety, immunogenicity and biomarker analyses. This included protocol and SAP input, TLF development and review, longitudinal and exploratory modelling, reproducible reporting, and end-to-end analysis of phosphorylated tau, neurofilament light, proteomics, microRNA and other complex biomarker data.

text:
Professional focus
My recent work spans global Phase III and real-world programs in immunology, autoimmune and inflammatory disease, nephrology, dermatology and allergology. Earlier leadership includes Phase I–II oncology and immuno-oncology, tau-immunotherapy studies in neurodegeneration, clinical pharmacology, vaccines, cardiovascular research and registry-based evidence.
I work at the intersection of biostatistics and statistical programming: shaping an analysis so that it is scientifically defensible, implementation-ready, reproducible and useful to clinical and medical teams.

title: R, R Shiny & Statistical Programming
text: I have 28 years of programming experience and use R as both a statistical language and an engineering platform for reproducible clinical and scientific work. My focus is not a tool in isolation, but the complete path from data and specifications to validated, interpretable outputs.

title: R, R Shiny & Statistical Programming
text:
Statistical programming


Clinical data and standards
Programming and extensive review of SDTM and ADaM datasets; creation and review of SDTM and ADaM specifications; review of define.xml; traceability from source data through analysis outputs.


TLF production and validation
Programming, double programming and review of tables, figures and listings; validation of SAS programs; independent reprogramming of selected SAS analyses in R.


Programming-ready SAPs
Writing and reviewing classical CSR-related SAPs and exploratory SAPs, with growing emphasis on specifications precise enough to support efficient, unambiguous statistical programming.

title: R, R Shiny & Statistical Programming
text:
End-to-end modernization
My workflows combine R, R Shiny, Quarto, interactive HTML, conditionally formatted Excel workbooks and presentation-ready outputs. I have connected analytical systems to SQL databases, including SQLite, and worked with Microsoft Azure and GitLab to support controlled, collaborative delivery.
The modernization principle is simple: analytical logic should be reusable, reviewable and consistent across data processing, statistical analysis, reporting and communication.

title: Leadership & Teaching
text: My career combines senior biopharma and CRO work with academic leadership, teaching, supervision and international scientific collaboration. I work comfortably across biostatistics, programming, data management, clinical and medical functions. I am an Officer and Treasurer of the International Society for Clinical Biostatistics (ISCB) and contribute to its international leadership and governance. View the ISCB Executive Committee →

title: Leadership & Teaching
text:
Leadership approach


Strategic thinking
Connect study objectives, estimands, design choices, data structures, analysis methods and reporting into one coherent evidence strategy.


 R-based technical modernization
Move teams toward reproducible R-based workflows, interactive reporting, reusable packages and clearer validation while respecting established regulatory processes.


Mentorship
Support statisticians, programmers, data scientists and students through review, training and practical collaboration at the boundary between methodology and implementation.

title: Leadership & Teaching
text:
International professional leadership


ISCB Executive Committee
Since 2026, I have served as an Officer and Treasurer of the International Society for Clinical Biostatistics (ISCB), contributing to the governance and financial stewardship of an international professional society connecting statistical methodology with clinical research.
View the ISCB Executive Committee →


Statistics in Regulatory Affairs
Since 2017, I have chaired the ISCB Statistics in Regulatory Affairs (SiRA) Subcommittee. SiRA reviews and comments on statistical aspects of regulatory requirements and guidance concerning data generation, collection, management, analysis and reporting. My work helps connect regulatory developments with the international clinical-biostatistics community.
Explore the SiRA Subcommittee and its work →


My earlier ISCB service included membership of the Executive Committee (2016–2019) and service as Acting Secretary and member of the National Groups Subcommittee (2016–2020).

title: Leadership & Teaching
text:
Academic profile

Associate Professor of Probability and Mathematical Statistics
Honorary Research Fellow and Research Associate, University of Glasgow
University teaching across multiple countries and institutions
Supervision of undergraduate, master’s, doctoral and research projects
Invited lectures, conference presentations and professional training
International research cooperation across universities, hospitals and research institutes

title: Leadership & Teaching
text:
Teaching themes
I teach statistics from mathematical foundations through study design, modelling and practical analysis. My principal teaching areas include:


Statistical foundations
Statistical inference, including estimation, hypothesis testing and the principles needed to select, apply and interpret statistical methods rigorously.


Design of studies
Statistical design of scientific and clinical studies, connecting research questions, study populations, endpoints, sample-size considerations and analysis strategies.


Statistical modelling
Linear statistical models, from core model formulation and diagnostics to interpretation and application in biomedical and scientific research.


Survival analysis
Methods for time-to-event data, including censoring, survival-function estimation, comparison of groups and regression modelling.


Multivariate methods
Analysis and interpretation of multiple correlated outcomes and high-dimensional observations, including dimension reduction and classification-oriented methods.


Spline smoothing
Flexible modelling of nonlinear relationships and curves using spline-based smoothing methods, with emphasis on principled model choice and interpretation.


These subjects are complemented by teaching and mentoring in applied biostatistics, R programming, reproducible research, statistical shape and image analysis, data science and the clear communication of statistical evidence. I have taught and supervised students at undergraduate, master’s and doctoral levels, as well as researchers and professionals working with biomedical data.

title: Leadership & Teaching
text:
Collaboration
I have collaborated with universities, university hospitals, research institutes, biotechnology companies, pharmaceutical organizations and CROs. These settings require different forms of leadership, but the common principle is the same: make complex analytical work understandable, reviewable and useful.
